transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. [Name], welcome in. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Thanks for seeing me. Um, so, the main reason I came in is, well, it's just getting really frustrating because I get pulled off track so easily. Like, incredibly easily. I’m a student right now, getting my bachelor's, but I also do some side projects and stuff, and it’s just... it’s like my brain has a million tabs open, you know? Like, I'll be working on something important, say, I'm supposed to be finishing up this data dashboard for a project, which I actually really like doing, but then—ping!—someone messages me on Slack. And instead of just ignoring it like a normal person, I have to check it. And then checking it reminds me of an email I need to send, which reminds me of a totally random idea for another project I want to start. Or even just, like, a song lyric will pop into my head, or I'll hear something outside, and suddenly I’ve completely lost the thread of what I was doing. I just drift away from the dashboard, and then an hour goes by, and I haven't gotten anywhere. It just happens all the time, and it's making everything take so much longer than it should.
Can you tell me if you've experienced this kind of distractibility for as long as you can remember, even back in childhood, or is this something that started more recently?

Oh, wow, yeah, definitely for as long as I can remember. It’s funny you ask that because I was actually just thinking about this the other day when I was trying to clean out some old boxes at my parents' house. My mom kept all these old report cards from when I was little—like, elementary school—and I was reading through them, and it’s honestly like reading about the exact same person I am now, just smaller. Every single year, my teachers would write these long comments on the back of the report card. It was never about me not understanding the material, but it was always, always about how I would just rush through my worksheets. Like, I’d get halfway through a math sheet and then just guess the rest because I was bored and wanted to do something else. 

And they always mentioned how I’d lose track of directions. The teacher would say, "Okay, first do this, then do that," and I’d maybe catch the first part, but by the second part, I was already looking out the window or playing with a pencil or something. And the group work! Oh my gosh, they were always saying I was too chatty and that I’d constantly talk over my classmates. I’d just get so excited about an idea, or I'd suddenly remember a story I wanted to tell, and I’d just blurt it out right in the middle of someone else talking. 

It was a whole thing at home, too. Homework was just a nightmare. My parents literally had to sit right next to me at the kitchen table every single night. If they didn’t, I would just wander off. Like, I’d get up to get a glass of water and end up in my room playing with Legos, completely forgetting that I had a spelling worksheet sitting on the table. Or I’d start one assignment, get distracted by the textbook for a different subject, and start reading that instead. So, yeah, this isn't new at all. It's just... it's just always been how my brain works, I guess. It's just harder to manage now that I'm in college and don't have my parents hovering over me to make sure I finish things.
Aside from the distractibility, do you often feel physically restless or fidgety, like you have trouble sitting still for long periods, even now as an adult?

Oh, absolutely. It's actually really annoying, and honestly, it can be just as exhausting as the distraction stuff. Like, especially with college, because there's so much sitting involved. If I have to sit still through a long Zoom call—like some of my seminar classes or those virtual study group meetings—or even if I'm just at the library trying to quietly work in one place, it gets so bad. 

After maybe twenty or thirty minutes, I start feeling this... this really uncomfortable pressure in my body. It's hard to explain, but it's almost like a coiled spring inside my chest and my legs, or like my skin is just slightly too tight? It just builds and builds, and I get this overwhelming feeling like I absolutely have to get up. If my camera is off on the Zoom call, I'm definitely up and pacing around my room while I listen. I'll just walk back and forth, or I'll start reorganizing my desk or folding laundry while the professor is talking, just to keep moving. 

But if my camera is on, or if I'm in a quiet place like the library where I can't just get up and pace around without looking weird, it's pretty much torture. I have to do something with my hands to let that pressure out. I'll be constantly spinning my pen, or peeling the label off my water bottle into tiny little strips, or I'll be aggressively bouncing my leg under the desk. Which I know drives my friends crazy when we study together because it literally shakes the whole table, but I almost don't even realize I'm doing it until someone points it out. 

And it's not even just when I'm working, either! Even if I'm watching a movie I actually really want to watch, sitting on the couch for two hours straight is just so hard for me. I'll end up shifting positions a million times, sitting with my legs over the back of the chair, or getting up to get a snack even if I'm not hungry, just to break up the sitting. It’s like my body just doesn't know how to be in "standby mode," you know? There's always this hum of energy that needs to go somewhere, and if I force myself to just sit completely still, that physical pressure just gets so intense that I can't even focus on what I'm supposed to be paying attention to anyway. So yeah, I'm pretty much always moving in some way.

Would you say these difficulties with focus and restlessness have caused real problems for you in more than one area of your life—like your schoolwork, your job or side projects, and your relationships with friends or family?

Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. It’s honestly why I finally decided I needed to come talk to somebody, because it’s not just a minor annoyance anymore, it’s actually starting to really mess things up for me across the board. 

Like with my side projects... I do some small freelance design and data stuff on the side, just to build up my resume and get some real-world experience, you know? But it's been... well, it's been really rocky. I had this one contract a few months ago for a local business wanting a simple inventory dashboard. I was so excited, I had all these great ideas, and the initial meetings went perfectly. But then, when it came to actually finishing the final, boring tweaks and sending everything over cleanly... I just kept getting sidetracked, or I'd get that restless feeling and have to go pace around my room instead of just sitting down to export the files. I kept telling them, "I'll have it to you tomorrow," and then I just wouldn't. Eventually, they just pulled the plug and went with someone else. And that's not the only time—I've actually lost a few small freelance contracts exactly like that, just because people realized they couldn't rely on me to follow through cleanly on the final steps. 

And it completely ruined this huge opportunity for me last semester, too. There was this portfolio competition for my major, and it was a huge deal because the winner gets this amazing mentorship. I had the pieces! My professors even told me my concepts were incredibly strong. But the submission required all these specific formatting rules and a detailed written statement, and I just... I completely missed out on it. I started the application, got totally sidetracked by redesigning my own personal logo for the thousandth time instead of writing the statement, and then the deadline just blew right past me. It was devastating, honestly, because I know I could have done really well if I had just been able to focus and submit the thing properly.

And it definitely bleeds into my relationships, too, especially with my friends from my program. Like, I have this core group of friends, and we always talk about collaborating. They always tell me they love my ideas—I'm usually the one they come to when they're brainstorming because I can always think of something out of the box. But when it comes to actually partnering up for a group project or a hackathon or something? I can tell they get really hesitant to actually work with me. It really hurts, but I also kind of can't blame them, you know? Because they've seen me promise to handle a section of a project, and then I end up doing it at 3 AM the night before, or I miss a crucial detail because I couldn't sit still long enough to actually proofread what I did. So now they kind of gently steer me away from the critical tasks, or they just politely find other partners. It's just incredibly frustrating because I want to be reliable, I really do, but it just feels like my own brain is sabotaging me in literally every part of my life right now.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient endorses a longstanding (since early elementary school), pervasive pattern of both inattentive symptoms (losing track of multi-step directions, careless errors/guessing on work, distractibility by internal and external stimuli, difficulty sustaining attention on tasks, forgetfulness/leaving tasks unfinished) and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (subjective restlessness, need to move/pace, fidgeting, difficulty remaining seated, blurting out/interrupting others, discomfort with 'standby mode'). Symptoms were present before age 12 (documented via childhood report cards) and have persisted into adulthood, causing clear functional impairment across multiple domains (academic performance, freelance work reliability, peer/collaborative relationships). The combination of significant inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptom clusters, each meeting sufficient symptom count and impact, supports the Combined Presentation (F90.2) rather than a predominantly inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive subtype.
